strengths: Addresses an important and timely safety problem in LLMs with clear practical motivation
Provides valuable empirical insight into why naive token-level attribution fails for long-form outputs (Appendix B.1), supported by concrete evidence
Demonstrates meaningful safety improvements on retrained models (Table 4: ASR reduction from 93.3% to 86.7%), not just detection metrics
Comprehensive evaluation across two different scenarios (jailbreaking and gender bias) and multiple datasets (ToxicChat, XSTest-Response) showing versatility
Good empirical results with 7.5% AUPRC improvement over state-of-the-art classifiers in jailbreaking detection
Honest discussion of limitations including injection setup assumptions, lack of fine-grained taxonomy, and adversarial robustness vulnerabilities
Well-structured analysis with useful ablation studies on validation set size (Figure 2) and token-level gradient contributions (Table 8)
weaknesses: Critical circularity issue: The method claims to avoid classifier requirements but still requires Llama-Guard-3-8B for screening and human annotation of ~200 samples for the primary jailbreaking scenario, partially undermining the core value proposition
Artificial experimental setup with unrealistic 0.025% injection ratios; evaluation on naturally-occurring unsafe data is absent, limiting real-world applicability
Strong and unaddressed validation set dependency: performance drops from AUPRC 0.50 (n=30) to 0.26 (n=3) without guidance on obtaining diverse validation data in practice
No computational cost analysis or scalability evaluation despite gradient computation over 41,573 training samples; applicability to million-scale datasets unknown

Limited technical novelty: applies standard gradient similarity method (Pruthi et al., 2020) with ad-hoc engineering solution (external classifier for targeted attribution) rather than principled improvements

Insufficient reproducibility details: 'optimizer-aware training gradients' mentioned but unexplained, random projection procedure not specified, human annotation protocol not detailed, code availability not mentioned
GradSafe (most relevant gradient-based baseline) lacks thorough comparison explaining why DABUF is superior beyond methodological differences in attribution targets

Gender bias evaluation less convincing: Ada3 is general-purpose baseline (not specialized for safety), D_target construction vaguely described, Table 7 shows Ada3 filtering worsens bias, suggesting detection metrics don't correlate with actual safety improvement
No ablation studies on critical hyperparameters (K=100 chosen arbitrarily; sensitivity to |D_identified| size unexplored)
Small test sets (|D_test|=30 for ToxicChat, 20 for XSTest) without error bars or significance testing; small validation sets undermine statistical reliability

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem of detecting unsafe training data in LLMs with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two distinct scenarios (jailbreaking and gender bias) with multiple baseline categories
Strong results on model safety metrics (Table 4: ASR reduction from 93.3% to 86.7% on ToxicChat after filtering)
Useful ablation studies and analysis (Appendix B) on token-wise gradient noise and validation set size effects
Honest discussion of limitations including homogeneous injections, lack of fine-grained taxonomy, and adversarial vulnerabilities
weaknesses: Contradicts main claim: method critically depends on moderation classifiers (Llama-Guard-3-8B) for candidate identification plus human annotation, undermining claimed independence from classifiers

Inconsistent detection performance: AUPRC on XSTest-Response is 74.1% (DABUF-Llama) vs 85.9% (Wildguard), a significant gap that is downplayed; method doesn't consistently outperform baselines on core detection metrics

Mixed results with different metrics: Claims superiority based on ASR after retraining (Table 4) while detection quality (AUPRC, precision, recall in Tables 2-3) is mixed, suggesting metric cherry-picking

Unrealistic experimental setup: homogeneous injections, extremely low injection ratios (0.025% jailbreaking, 1.5% bias), and artificial validation scenarios don't reflect real-world unsafe data distributions

Validation set leakage concerns: Using D_test to compute influences for training data detection may lead to overfitting; Figure 2 shows high variance with small validation sets but no sensitivity analysis on which specific examples are used

Critical reproducibility issues: Human annotation process barely described (no inter-annotator agreement, annotation guidelines, or disagreement resolution procedure); no code availability mentioned; essential implementation details missing

Limited novelty: Gradient similarity attribution (Pruthi et al. 2020, Xia et al. 2024) is not new; main contribution reduces to applying existing techniques with classifier-filtered validation—appears incremental
Statistical rigor gaps: Main results (Tables 2, 3, 4) lack error bars, significance tests, or multiple runs; small validation sets suggest high variance but this isn't quantified
Unclear practical advantage: Method pipeline (classification → annotation → gradients → filtering) seems more expensive than alternatives; computational cost never compared to baselines
Gender bias experiments differ fundamentally: Uses mislabeled data rather than unsafe content; comparison to Ada3 (general embeddings) is unfair; no comparison to fairness literature methods

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in LLM safety with clear motivation and a pragmatic solution
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two different safety scenarios (jailbreaking and gender bias) with multiple models, datasets, and baselines
Strong empirical results where retrained models show meaningful improvements in safety, which is the most important practical metric
Insightful analysis of why naive data attribution fails for long-form outputs, with detailed token-level analysis demonstrating the noise from benign tokens overwhelming unsafe signals
Versatility demonstrated across heterogeneous safety concerns without requiring predefined taxonomies, unlike existing classifiers
Well-structured paper with thorough experimental details, good ablation studies in appendices, and appropriate metrics (AUPRC, precision, recall, F1, ASR, TPR Gender Gap)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily applies existing gradient similarity attribution with existing LLM classifiers; the main contribution is using classifier-identified data as attribution targets rather than model outputs, which is a pragmatic but incremental insight

Circular dependency concern: uses Llama-Guard-3-8B to create the attribution target for jailbreaking, then evaluates against Llama-Guard and related classifiers, potentially biasing results and making it unclear how much improvement comes from DABUF vs. Llama-Guard's limitations

Heavy reliance on auxiliary components undermines core claims: method still requires Llama-Guard + human annotation of ~200 samples, contradicting the claimed advantage over classifier-based approaches; human annotation overhead not thoroughly analyzed

Narrow experimental scope: only two application scenarios, two unsafe datasets for jailbreaking, homogeneous injection setup (acknowledged as unrealistic), no fine-grained detection taxonomy, and limited analysis of failure cases

Missing key comparisons: no direct comparison to simple baselines (e.g., just filtering top-100 by Llama-Guard), making it unclear how much value attribution adds; gender bias evaluation only compares to Ada3 embeddings, which weren't designed for this task
Attribution method choices underexplored: random projection dimension (d=8192) lacks justification, no sensitivity analysis, and known limitations of gradient similarity not thoroughly discussed
Validation set size creates hyperparameter dependency (Figure 2) that requires tuning; inconsistent across experiments (30 for ToxicChat, not specified clearly for others)
Acknowledged limitations not resolved: homogeneous injection unrealistic, no fine-grained taxonomy support, vulnerability to adversarial attacks on attribution (Wang et al., 2024d) not addressed
Limited error analysis: no qualitative investigation of which unsafe data types DABUF misses, false positive rates, or failure mode analysis
Scalability concerns: human annotation requirements, computational cost of computing gradients for large training sets, and practical deployment details not thoroughly discussed

strengths: Clear identification and visualization of the 'noisy representation' problem in existing methods, with compelling t-SNE visualizations demonstrating the effectiveness of denoising
Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks: up to 63.3% AUPRC improvement and 39.9% ASR reduction after retraining, outperforming SOTA LLM-based classifiers
Solid theoretical grounding using signal detection theory (discriminability index d') and connection to optimal linear detection scores

Comprehensive experimental design with proper evaluation pipeline (detection → filtering → retraining), multiple baselines from four categories, ablation studies, and evaluation on diverse unsafe scenarios (jailbreaks, gender bias)
Practical effectiveness with minimal data requirements: achieves strong performance with as few as 3 target examples
Honest discussion of limitations without overselling; good acknowledgment of assumptions and potential risks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method combines well-established techniques (PCA whitening, dimension reduction, discriminability-based selection) without introducing fundamentally new concepts; primarily an engineering contribution
Core assumption (μQ ≈ μU alignment) is crucial but unvalidated: no empirical measurement of approximation quality or analysis of failure modes when target and unsafe distributions diverge
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: r=30 for dimension selection and m' selection procedure are not specified or studied; no sensitivity analysis provided despite potential impact on results

Limited experimental scope: homogeneous injection setup (all unsafe data from single distribution) doesn't reflect real-world heterogeneous scenarios; only two unsafe types tested; gender bias experiment uses only 150 samples with single corruption pattern

Target set construction is underspecified and non-trivial in practice: unclear which unsafe model outputs to include or how to ensure coverage; Figure 3 shows sensitivity to target size but provides no guidance on minimum diversity requirements

Missing statistical rigor: main results lack confidence intervals or significance testing; standard deviations only in appendix; some large performance gains (e.g., 88.5% → 98.6%) lack statistical validation
Computational cost analysis absent: no runtime/memory requirements; scalability to large datasets unclear; covariance matrix computation could be expensive for high-dimensional representations
Incomplete analysis of failure modes: GradSim achieves only 1.7% on XSTest but 41.1% on ToxicChat—why? No exploration of when DRA fails or which unsafe patterns are hardest to detect
Conceptual framing issue: 'denoising' terminology is somewhat misleading; this is primarily discriminability-aware dimension selection rather than classical denoising approaches
Reproducibility concerns: target set construction procedure for retraining ('union across 10 runs') not fully specified; no code availability mentioned; some details relegated to appendix only

strengths: Clear and intuitive problem motivation: identifies concrete limitation in existing methods where averaging representations over all tokens introduces noise
Strong empirical results: demonstrates consistent AUPRC improvements of 23-63% over baselines and reduces ASR by up to 39.9% through retraining
Theoretical grounding in signal detection theory provides principled justification via discriminability index d' and optimal linear detection scores
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including two unsafe scenarios (jailbreaking and gender bias), multiple baseline categories, ablation studies, and analysis of target set size effects
Practical efficiency with minimal target data: works effectively with as few as 3 examples, outperforming Wildguard in low-resource settings
Consistent improvements across two different model architectures (Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: applies standard ML techniques (centering/whitening normalization, PCA-based dimension selection) to new problem rather than proposing genuinely new methods
Critical unvalidated assumption: assumes µQ ≈ µU without theoretical or empirical justification; unclear when this assumption holds or fails in practice

Artificial experimental setup: assumes homogeneous unsafe data injection from single distribution, which is unrealistic; paper acknowledges this but doesn't address robustness to heterogeneous contamination
Incomplete technical details: hyperparameter r=30 appears fixed without justification or sensitivity analysis; m' selection unexplained; dimension search procedure not clearly specified

Circular evaluation in gender bias experiment: target set Dtarget constructed from model outputs trained on contaminated data, potentially introducing circularity rather than testing true generalization
Missing robustness analysis: no investigation of adversarial attacks mentioned in limitations; no analysis of failure modes or robustness to out-of-distribution unsafe examples
Theoretical gaps: leave-target-out surrogate d'_LTO lacks theoretical grounding; no analysis of approximation error when replacing µU with µQ in optimal weights
Limited baseline comparisons: only two model architectures tested; missing comparisons with recent safe data filtering methods; GradSafe comparison dismissed rather than addressed rigorously
Evaluation concerns: ASR via LLM-as-judge potentially noisy and expensive; no statistical significance testing on main results; no computational cost analysis vs. baselines
Artificial contamination scale: gender bias experiment uses only 1.5% contamination ratio (150/10000); unclear how method scales with different contamination levels

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper identifies a concrete limitation in existing representation-based methods (noise from neutral tokens) and articulates this clearly with good visualizations.

Theoretically grounded approach: Uses signal detection theory to motivate the method, connecting to classical optimal linear detection results (Lemma 3.1) and deriving discriminability index d' as a principled objective.
Strong empirical results: Achieves 63.3% average AUPRC improvement over baselines and 39.9% ASR reduction after retraining, with consistent gains across model architectures (Llama, Gemma).
Comprehensive evaluation: Tests on two distinct task scenarios with multiple baselines, both detection (AUPRC) and downstream safety metrics (ASR, TPR Gender Gap), plus ablation studies.
Practical utility: Simple two-step approach requiring no additional labeled data or model training, with clear applicability to safety-critical scenarios.
Good visualization and analysis: Figures 1-2 clearly demonstrate noise reduction; Figure 3 shows target set size effects; ablation studies show both components contribute.
Reproducibility: Detailed experimental setup, hyperparameters, and standard libraries specified; code availability promised.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Centering and whitening are standard statistical techniques; Lemma 3.1 is classical signal detection theory (Poor 2013); main contribution is applying known techniques rather than developing novel theory.

Unvalidated critical assumption: Method assumes µQ ≈ µU (target set mean equals unsafe training data mean), but this is neither justified nor validated. No robustness analysis when this assumption is violated, particularly when target responses and training unsafe data have different distributions.

Narrow experimental scope: All experiments use artificially injected unsafe data with clear patterns, not naturally occurring unsafe training data. Limited to two scenarios (jailbreaking, gender bias); gender bias experiment uses only 150 samples from 10k benign.

Target set dependency: Strong dependence on target set size (Figure 3) with performance degradation at small sizes. Requires expensive red teaming; provides minimal guidance on target set selection in practice.

Hyperparameter selection unjustified: Dimension size r=30 used without justification or sensitivity analysis. Choice of m' not specified. No computational cost analysis despite potential C(m', r) combinations.

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of which dimensions are selected and why they're effective. No error analysis or failure case discussion. No computational cost comparison. Missing analysis of when method breaks down.

Leave-target-out surrogate concerns: Using d'_LTO as proxy for detecting unsafe training data is indirect and conflates different objectives. No validation that target set distribution matches unsafe training data distribution.
Evaluation protocol concerns: Target set D_target composed as union across 10 runs, making composition variable. No cross-validation analysis; unclear if results are sensitive to target set seeds.

Limited baselines: Only one model-free method (GradSafe); missing recent data attribution baselines and simple threshold baselines. Gender bias baseline (Wildguard 0.059 AUPRC) too weak to be meaningful.
Adversarial robustness not addressed: Paper acknowledges Wang et al. (2024b) on adversarial attacks against data attribution but provides no defense analysis or adversarial evaluation experiments.
